front: According to Fedorova, how low can processor pipeline utilization fall, and for what workloads?
back: As low as 19%: modern workloads with frequent branches and control transfers can push it that low (abstract), and even some SPEC CPU benchmarks yield 19% for some configurations (Section 1).

text: Fedorova defines CMT (chip multithreading) as a processor architecture combining {{c1::chip multiprocessing (CMP)}} and {{c2::hardware multithreading (MT)}}.

front: When did hardware vendors plan to ship CMT systems, per Fedorova's abstract?
back: "Within the next two years", i.e. around 2005; the paper is written ahead of the hardware.

front: What is Fedorova's headline simulation result for a CMT-savvy OS scheduler?
back: It could improve application performance by a factor of two. The paper is an initial analysis plus a proposed scheduler design, not a finished scheduler.

front: Which workloads does Fedorova name as having poor CPU pipeline utilization?
back: Application servers, web services, and on-line transaction processing (OLTP); they run many threads of short integer stretches with frequent dynamic branches, hurting cache locality and branch prediction and causing frequent stalls.

front: Per Fedorova, what workloads do superscalar speculative/out-of-order processors help, and which do they not?
back: They extract instruction-level parallelism (ILP) from scientific workloads but can do little for transaction-processing-like workloads.

front: Why were CMP and MT designed, according to Fedorova's introduction?
back: To improve utilization for transaction-processing-like workloads by better supporting thread-level parallelism (TLP).

text: Fedorova defines a {{c1::CMP}} processor as putting multiple cores on one chip so more than one thread is active at a time, and an {{c2::MT}} processor as having multiple sets of registers and thread state and interleaving instructions from different threads.
extra: An MT processor either switches between threads (as often as each cycle) or executes instructions from multiple threads simultaneously if they use different functional units.

front: State the latency-hiding principle as Fedorova gives it.
back: If one thread is blocked on a memory access or other long-latency operation, other threads can make forward progress.

front: Which contemporary hardware does Fedorova cite as CMP systems, and which as an MT system?
back: CMP: IBM's Power4 and Sun's UltraSPARC IV. MT: Intel's hyper-threaded Xeon.

front: What prior evidence on MT scheduling does Fedorova cite in Section 1?
back: An OS scheduler tailored for MT processors produced an average 17% performance improvement; and a naive scheduler can make a multithreaded processor perform worse than a single-threaded one.

front: What is Fedorova's scalability thesis for CMT scheduling?
back: Scheduler designs proposed for single-processor multithreaded systems do not scale to the dozens of hardware threads expected on CMT processors, so CMT needs a fundamentally new scheduler design.

front: How does Fedorova define an ideal scheduler?
back: It assigns threads to processors so as to minimize resource contention and maximize system throughput, scalably, and it must understand how its decisions affect resource contention because contention ultimately determines performance.

front: How did prior single-processor MT scheduling algorithms work (Fedorova, Section 2)?
back: They ran all combinations of threads that could be co-scheduled, measured which combinations performed best, and used that data for later decisions.

front: Why do the combination-trying MT algorithms not scale, per Fedorova's example?
back: An OLTP workload may have a hundred threads, and on a CMT system with 16 hardware contexts there are 10^27 combinations to evaluate.

front: What second scaling problem does Fedorova note for combination-trying schedulers?
back: While the scheduler evaluates schedules it is bound to try bad ones, during which the system does not run at best performance.

front: What alternative scheduling approach does Fedorova propose in Section 2?
back: A scheduler that models relative resource contention from different potential schedules and uses that as the basis for decisions, rather than trying combinations empirically.

front: What hybrid does Fedorova suggest, conceding that modeling resource contention is hard?
back: Use the contention model to shrink the problem space, then fall back on the earlier combination-trying algorithms for the final decision.

front: What simulator does Fedorova use, and what is it built on?
back: A CMT toolkit built as a set of extensions to the Simics simulation toolkit. The cores per chip and degree of hardware multithreading are configurable.

front: Fedorova's simulated core uses fine-grained multithreading after Laudon et al. How many hardware contexts does it usually have, and how often does it switch?
back: Usually one, two, four, or eight hardware contexts (each a set of registers and thread state); the processor interleaves instructions from the threads and switches contexts on every cycle.

front: In Fedorova's model, what happens when one or more threads are blocked?
back: The system keeps switching among the remaining available threads (e.g. while one services a cache miss); this is the mechanism behind latency hiding.

front: Describe the simulated core and cache layout in Fedorova's platform.
back: A simple RISC pipeline with one set of functional units (arithmetic, load/store, etc.), typically four hardware contexts per core. Each core has a single shared TLB and L1 data and instruction caches; the integrated L2 cache is shared by all cores on the chip.

front: What does Fedorova call a design with multiple sets of functional units on each core, and why did the authors not build it?
back: A simultaneous multithreaded (SMT) system; SMT is more complex and needs more chip real estate.

front: What core design did Fedorova's authors use instead of SMT, and what tradeoff does it make?
back: A simple classical RISC core, to fit more cores per chip; it trades per-core capability for a higher degree of multithreading and higher throughput on multithreaded and multiprogrammed workloads.

front: Why do ALU instructions have 0 delay latency in Fedorova's modeled pipeline?
back: The modeled pipeline implements result bypassing (footnote 1).

text: In Fedorova's terminology, each hardware context appears to the OS as a {{c1::logical processor}}, and a software thread is assigned to a hardware context for the duration of a {{c2::scheduling time slice}}.

front: Which contended resource does Fedorova's study focus on, and why?
back: The processor pipeline, because pipeline contention is what distinguishes single-threaded from multithreaded processors.

front: Define instruction delay latency as Fedorova uses it.
back: When a thread performs a long-latency operation it is blocked, and subsequent instructions from that thread are delayed until the operation completes; the delay's duration is the instruction delay latency.

front: State Fedorova's contention rule relating instruction type to pipeline contention.
back: A thread dominated by long-delay-latency instructions (memory loads) leaves functional units unused, so contention is low; a thread of strictly ALU operations keeps the pipeline busy and co-scheduled threads suffer.

front: What are the theoretical lower and upper performance bounds in Fedorova's three-system comparison?
back: A conventional single-threaded core is the lower bound; a traditional multiprocessor is the upper bound. When contention is low an MT core approaches MP performance; when contention is high an MT core is no better than a single-threaded processor.

front: Describe the workloads and systems in Fedorova's Section 4 worked example.
back: Two workloads: four ALU-only threads (0-cycle delay latency) and four load-only threads (4-cycle delay latency), run across three systems: A single-threaded, B four-context multithreaded, C four-way multiprocessor.

front: What is Fedorova's CPU-bound result across systems A, B, and C (Figure 1)?
back: A and B perform comparably; C is four times faster because it has four times as many functional units.

front: What is Fedorova's memory-bound result across systems A, B, and C (Figure 2)?
back: B and C perform comparably and beat A by a factor of four, because B and C overlap the four threads' memory-access latencies (assuming cache hit rate and memory bandwidth on B are no worse than on A or C, footnote 2).

front: How did Fedorova validate the contention theory in simulation (Figure 3)?
back: With hand-crafted instruction mixes (strictly ALU for CPU-bound, strictly load for memory-bound), with throughput normalized to System A.

front: What heuristic does Fedorova propose for approximating a workload's pipeline requirements, and what co-scheduling does it imply?
back: Instruction mix, and more precisely average instruction delay latency, can serve as the heuristic; the scheduler should co-schedule a long-latency-dominated thread with a short-latency, high-functional-unit-demand thread.

front: What limits of the instruction-delay-latency heuristic does Fedorova state?
back: It is only a heuristic, does not model contention for other resources, and so does not always predict performance; in particular it ignores cache contention when threads with large working sets share a processor.

front: What does Fedorova's working-set experiment (8 bytes to 2MB, Figure 4) reveal?
back: The simple heuristic predicts B and C perform comparably, but in the middle of the graph the two curves diverge, caused by the reduced L1 data-cache hit rate on B where four threads share the cache. Early evidence that cache, not just pipeline, matters.

front: What extension to the model were Fedorova's authors working on at the time of Section 4?
back: Extending the model to include cache contention and cooperative data sharing.

text: In Fedorova's Table 1, schedule {{c1::(a)}} runs every core at CPIs 1, 6, 11, 16, while schedule {{c2::(d)}} runs cores at 1,1,1,1 / 6,6,6,6 / 11,11,11,11 / 16,16,16,16.

front: Fedorova's summary says CPI-based scheduling works well for simple workloads. What is its first stated limitation?
back: CPI does not give precise information on the types of instructions executed, so using CPI alone the scheduler cannot tell which threads will compete for other resources such as the cache hierarchy or a floating-point unit.

front: Per Fedorova's summary, how much performance may a naive scheduler squander on CMT, and what does the proposed CPI-based scheduler gain over it?
back: A naive scheduler may squander up to half of available application performance; the CPI-based scheduler yields a two-fold improvement over a naive one.

front: Which CPI-related follow-on topics were Fedorova's authors investigating?
back: Inferring single-threaded CPI from CMT CPI; and studying the nature and dynamics of CPIs in real workloads to see whether CPI is viable for real applications.

front: Which follow-on topics beyond CPI did Fedorova's authors list for workload characterization?
back: Determining the effects of cache contention on co-scheduled throughput; and using other workload characteristics such as static instruction mix.

front: Besides new metrics, what two follow-on steps did Fedorova's authors list for their scheduler ideas?
back: Integrating the ideas with other scheduling policies, and testing on real workloads.
